newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Embarrassed Swiss say goodbye to Marshal Mobutu.
newsitem.headline: Embarrassed Swiss say goodbye to Marshal Mobutu.

text.p: Switzerland breathed a sigh of relief on Tuesday with the end of Zaire President Mobutu Sese Seko's embarrassing presence. He was like an unwanted guest who stayed too long.
Marshal Mobutu quietly left Switzerland on Monday for the French Riviera after two-and-half months of cancer therapy in the serene town of Lausanne, where he stayed at the palatial Beau-Rivage hotel.

But some Swiss politicians said they were mobilising to prevent a return of the man whose visit added to the image problems of the neutral Alpine country, accused by Jewish lobby groups around the world of cosying up to the wartime Nazis.
Mobutu, whose current Swiss visa expires on November 27, was "beefed up" and given a drug boost by his doctors for the trip to France and may slip back here for treatment, diplomats said.

The Swiss foreign ministry would not say if Mobutu was welcome to come back. "This is a question we cannot answer now," said spokesman Jean-Philippe Tissieres. "This question will be dealt with at the appropriate time if raised."

Swiss newspapers and parliamentarians said good riddance to the Zairean ruler, an international pariah banned from much of West Europe and the United States -- and with $4 billion in numbered Swiss bank accounts according to Swiss media.
"Auf Wiedersehen (until we meet again) -- he probably heard this farewell greeting from only a few," said the Zurich German-language daily Tages-Anzeiger.

It suggested that the small group of wellwishers might include the Lausanne hotel director whose luxury establishment earned nearly one million Swiss francs for his stay, and doctors "who experience shows know how to value private patients with fat wallets"
"But otherwise everyone will be glad he finally left."
Mobutu's spokesman Kabuya Lumuna says he will stay a while in France, where he has a villa in Nice, and then return home.
But Swiss parliamentarians were taking no chances and hoping to block his return to Switzerland.
Josef Zisyadis, a member of Lausanne's cantonal parliament, said he had heard security reports that Mobutu could come back.
To block this, cantonal deputies would vote for a motion asking the federal government to block Mobutu's return, he said.
"We're happy that this dictator is out of our city. But we want to make sure he won't come back," Zisyadis told Reuters.
"Mobutu's presence here was a scandal," he said. "It only reinforced an impression that Switzerland welcomes dictators with money. It was terrible for our national image."

Peter Vollmer, a member of the foreign affairs committee of the parliament's lower house, said the panel had made clear to Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti that Switzerland had to weigh very carefully whether it should let Mobutu back in.

In view of the attacks Switzerland is already facing, it could not afford "pictures of a blood-stained dictator going around the world from a Swiss luxury hotel", German-language daily Berner Zeitung quoted him as saying.
In a scathing commentary, Tages-Anzeiger speculated that Switzerland could be the scene of a protracted legal battle over Mobutu's personal fortune if he dies or is ousted.
"The perpetrator or his heirs who've robbed the country with criminal creativity will insist on their rights in civilised Switzerland. The victims will wait and wait and wait," it said.
Switzerland has been the scene of legal battles over bank accounts of fallen leaders including the late Philippine ruler Ferdinand Marcos and Haiti's Jean-Claude "Baby Doc" Duvalier.
